The Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China (Alliance) is charged with inciting subversion. Lee Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung, who pleaded not guilty, completed a 24-day trial, with the verdict delivered on 21 August. *The Collective* revisits the most striking scenes and exchanges in court, recapping the key points of their testimony. On 4 June 1997, in Victoria Park. Lee Cheuk-yan, wearing a black T-shirt printed with "Don't want to remember! Dare not forget!," took the microphone and read in English: "Some say this is the last candlelight vigil for our democratic movement, the last night for China's democracy. Dear compatriots, this is absolutely not true. After the handover, the Alliance will continue to hold the candlelight vigil in Victoria Park every year..." Lee Cheuk-yan was then 40, with dark hair and rounded cheeks. Nearly 30 years later, 68-year-old Lee, now white-haired, sat in the dock, watching himself on the screen, fists resting near his nose, lips pressed together, wiping tears with his fingers. This veteran Alliance member is charged with inciting subversion of state power. Having pleaded not guilty, he took the stand to testify about his June Fourth experience and the Alliance's beliefs. He wept while old video clips of the June Fourth vigils played, choked up when recalling the suffering of the grassroots, and made no secret that even after the National Security Law he still upheld the Five Core Demands—all because of "love for the people." Related reports on the Alliance case: Alliance Case · Trial Notes | Chow Hang-tung's "intention" / Alliance Case | 24-day trial, verdict on 21 Aug — a summary of nine key factual issues and legal points of contention

Lee Cheuk-yan was jailed in April 2021 over the 18 August 'flowing water' assembly case. By the time of the verdict, he had been deprived of liberty for over five years and four months.

Born into moderate prosperity, determined to shoulder responsibility for a China in苦难

On the 13th day of trial, white-haired Lee Cheuk-yan, wearing a dark grey long-sleeved shirt and black puffer vest, stepped into the witness box. He smiled and nodded to the public gallery, swore on the Catholic Bible, and began his testimony.

Lee Cheuk-yan's more than 40 years of trade-union and political work began in his university days. Entering the University of Hong Kong's civil engineering department in 1975, he encountered the "recognise China, concern society"思潮 (academic movement), and learned of Wei Jingsheng's call for a "fifth modernisation"—democracy. Coming from a comfortably-off family, he joined the hostel association and threw himself into grassroots movements, which had a profound impact on him.

Recalling visits to boat-dwellers, and how a child had drowned, he could not help choking up, as if the scene from over 40 years before had resurfaced. He said his generation was a product of the times: being born into a China in苦难 carried a responsibility. After graduation, he decided not to practise civil engineering, but to "do something" for Hong Kong society and for China.

"Under that background, I began my life's...," he smiled. "I never imagined it would turn out to be a lifetime." His leading counsel, Mr Shum, asked: "A lifetime of what?" Lee replied: "A lifetime of trade-union work, and concern for China's democracy."

Lee Cheuk-yan told the court that the "recognise China, concern society" academic思潮 during his university years had influenced him and led him to devote himself to grassroots causes, trade unions, and the democracy movement. (Facebook photo)

Baptism of June Fourth: supporting the democracy movement became a lifelong commitment

After that, Lee threw himself into trade-union work while continuing to follow China's democracy movement. When the 1989 pro-democracy movement erupted, the 32-year-old was working as an organiser at the Hong Kong Christian Industrial Committee. He recalled that after Hu Yaobang's death in April 1989, students gathered in Tiananmen Square to voice demands against official corruption and abuses, while Hongkongers marched to the Xinhua News Agency and staged sit-ins in solidarity; he was there serving as march marshal.

After the Beijing students went on hunger strike, over a million Hongkongers marched twice in support, and on 27 May the "Democratic Songs Dedicated to China" concert was held at Happy Valley racecourse, raising about HK$12 million. On 21 May, Szeto Wah announced the formation of the Alliance. A week or so later, Lee and other Alliance representatives took one million dollars in donations to Beijing.

After 4 June, Lee was detained. He said it was Hong Kong citizens demanding his release that saved him, and made him all the more determined to continue supporting China's democracy movement. (Facebook photo)

In Tiananmen Square, he saw students, workers and intellectuals fighting to have withdrawn the 26 April editorial that branded the movement a "turmoil." "They really wanted to tell the regime... we are patriots, we just want the country to be good—the patriotic sentiment at the time was extremely strong," he said. Late on the night of 3 June, while in the workers' tent, he was suddenly told to leave: "They said the troops had broken in and they were going out to block the soldiers." Back at the hotel, he did not sleep all night, "watching outside, hearing the gunfire, watching Tiananmen Square..." He fell silent for a moment. "Around four o'clock...lights out."

After 4 June, Lee withdrew with other supporters, students and journalists, but on the chartered flight back to Hong Kong, public-security officers ordered him off the plane. He was detained for two days; after his donations were confiscated and he signed a statement of remorse, he was allowed to return.

In Tiananmen Square he witnessed the dead and wounded being driven along Chang'an Avenue on tricycle carts; later he heard testimony of the massacre. He described 4 June as another baptism. "Beijing citizens told us they wanted the world to know what we had seen." During his detention, Hong Kong citizens had marched to the Governor's House and the Xinhua News Agency demanding his release: "It was Hong Kong citizens who saved me." After his return, he decided to continue supporting China's democracy movement and to help both China and Hong Kong move towards democracy: "I felt an even greater responsibility, a lifelong commitment."

After being detained, Lee Cheuk-yan had his donations confiscated and signed a statement of remorse before being allowed to return to Hong Kong. Signing that statement became the regret of his life. (Facebook photo)

Upholding the Five Core Demands: dictatorship vs democracy are opposites

The Alliance's full name is the "Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China." Formally established in early June 1989, Lee Cheuk-yan was among its first standing committee members. He explained that the organisation's role was to support movements launched inside China, welcoming all like-minded people, including pro-Beijing groups; it had always been peaceful and non-violent, and prior to 2020 had received a letter of no objection from the police for every annual June Fourth vigil.

Lee said the Five Core Demands that the Alliance had consistently upheld had never changed—they were "ring upon ring." First, release those imprisoned; then recognise the movement as a patriotic democratic one, and acknowledge that the massacre and suppression were wrong, and pursue accountability; and pass on the 1989 movement's demands that one-party rule be ended so that people could enjoy freedoms of speech, association and the press, and a civil society be built—only then would there be a foundation for discussing democracy and the system best suited to China. He explained that dictatorship concentrated executive, legislative and judicial powers to suppress and punish the people's voice, and was the antithesis of democracy; without ending dictatorship, building a democratic China would be "absolutely impossible."

Lee emphasised the Alliance played a supporting role; it had not discussed what system China should adopt—things had not reached that stage at all: "If China has no freedom, if the people have no freedom, there is nothing to discuss." He also disagreed with the equation "end one-party dictatorship" with "end Communist Party leadership": "Whether the Communist Party leads is not for us to say; it is for the people to say."

The Alliance was established in early June 1989, and Lee Cheuk-yan (first right) was among its first standing-committee members. (File photo)

Relaxed expression, smiling answers to challenging questions

Throughout his testimony, Lee appeared relaxed and spoke calmly, much as he had countless times before the media. He fielded every question with ease and directness, sometimes with a touch of humour.

When the prosecution asked if he wished the Chinese Communist Party to remain in power, he laughed and spread his hands: "Disagree—it's for the people to decide. We're not in a position to agree or disagree." When the prosecution suggested he believed intra-party reform within the CCP could not end one-party dictatorship, he again disagreed, smiling: "Don't pigeonhole the Communist Party like that," drawing laughter from the public gallery.

When the judge asked if he had paid attention to China's 2018 constitutional amendment, he laughed and said: "Frankly, no, because I think the Communist Party's leadership is a constant—I don't need to [follow it]." He added: "I did notice they crammed in 'Communist Party leadership.' My reaction was—do they need to? Everyone knows that already." As to whether he wanted more people to act on "end one-party dictatorship," he said the question was a false one: "If we're calling on people to act, we won't say 'do things to end one-party dictatorship.' We won't put it that way."

In 2018 the state amended the constitution; the prosecution alleges that one of the Five Core Demands—"end one-party dictatorship"—is equivalent to ending Communist Party leadership and is thus an unlawful means that breaches the national constitution.

"I have no enmity in my heart, only love"

The prosecution challenged Lee twice in court over alleged enmity towards the CCP. The first time, Deputy Senior Prosecutor Lai Ka-yi asked whether he bore "great enmity" towards CCP rule. Lee shook his head: "Disagree." Lai rephrased: "At least some enmity." Lee immediately replied: "I have no enmity in my heart, only love. It is out of love for the people—I hope the Communist Party can reform so that people can enjoy the rights and happiness they deserve."

The second time, Lai suggested that by continually advocating "end one-party dictatorship," Lee wanted more people to harbour enmity towards the CCP. He denied this again, stressing that he wanted the public to have expectations of the CCP, hoping it would respect democracy and human rights—"it should not be called enmity."

Lai asked Lee a series of questions about his views on the CCP. "Do you agree that the Alliance and you have always regarded the Chinese Communist Party as an authoritarian regime?" Lee tilted his head, thought for a few seconds and replied: "Before '49 it wasn't an authoritarian regime; after the country was founded it became one." He went on to agree with each of the prosecution's other characterisations: that the Alliance regarded the CCP as "strangling the people's voice, especially dissenting voices," "strangling democracy," "suppressing the people through the state system," "violating human rights," "offering no genuine elections in which the people truly participate," and treating the "Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference as a token body."

"So do you agree that the Alliance believed the Chinese Communist Party's rule of the country was, in practice, one-party dictatorship?" "I agree, but it shouldn't be a one-party dictatorship," Lee said.

Lee Cheuk-yan denied harbouring enmity towards the CCP, saying: "I have no enmity in my heart, only love."

"Of course I am absolutely patriotic"

After Lee denied enmity towards CCP rule, the prosecution switched tack, suggesting he bore "dissatisfaction" with it and believed CCP rule was "bad for the country." Lee said he "praised what should be praised and criticised what should be criticised"—there were policies he welcomed and ones he did not, with the greatest dissatisfaction being "the people have no voice, no basic rights." He also openly acknowledged that he had learned trade-union work from the Communist Party: "When I was young, I greatly admired the Communist Party."

Pressed repeatedly by the prosecution, he said: "It's bad for the country, but we hope it will be better for the country and the people," adding: "I stress again, I hope it does well." Judge Andrew Chan asked: "Meaning the Communist Party?" Lee replied: "Yes, I hope the Communist Party does well."

Loving the country does not equal loving the Party—a useful lens, perhaps, for understanding the Alliance's beliefs. In its opening, the prosecution noted that at a protest in 2012, Lee had said: "We are absolutely patriotic, but if we are to love the country, we must end one-party dictatorship—that is what true patriotism is."

Lee's counsel, in his final question in chief, asked: the Alliance's full name includes the word "patriotic"—does he love the country?

"I think from the moment I entered university, I already felt that a China in苦难 needed a tomorrow. From then on I hoped the country would develop towards prosperity, democracy and freedom, and resolved to work for a better future for its people. Of course, I am absolutely patriotic," Lee said.

Asked whether he loved his country, Lee said he was "absolutely patriotic," and that from his first days at university he had hoped the country would become prosperous, democratic and free. (File photo)
